title: Black and African cinema hub opens in London
content:
A new black and African cinema and hub has officially opened in south-west London.
EbonyLife Place, based near Nine Elms, was unveiled with a ceremony attended by the Mayor of London Lord Khan, and its founder Mo Abudu.
Abudu, a Nigerian media mogul who was born in London, explained that the project was born from a desire to showcase and celebrate stories that she felt previously lacked a home.
"I do think there is a younger audience of young people now that just want to see great storytelling," Abudu said.
She added: "We make great films, and I think we need to create experiences where people can come and they can see the great work that we do in black cinema, in African cinema.
"We don't have enough spaces to serve black cinema in the United Kingdom... representation is so important to us."
At the heart of the cultural centre is a 160-seat auditorium featuring a year-round film programme.
The screenings will primarily focus on Nollywood cinema from Nigeria alongside other movies connecting to the black experience.
In addition to film screenings, the venue will host masterclasses, industry panels, and live performances by established and emerging talent.
Beyond its cinema space, the multi-storey venue features a bar, a lounge called "Fàhinti" (a Yoruba word meaning to lean back and rest), a Nigerian restaurant, a boutique showcasing African and diaspora designers, and walls lined with African diaspora artwork.
The project, financed almost entirely by Abudu's media group, mirrors the upscale lifestyle complex she launched in Nigeria's biggest city, Lagos, in 2019.
Speaking at Thursday's launch, Lord Khan said: "London is the number one place in Europe to film," adding that the capital sits just behind Los Angeles and ahead of New York in the global film production footprint.
"As long as I'm mayor, we'll invest in culture," he said.
The opening coincides with the London Film Festival.

title: BBC to cut raft of Radio 4 programmes including You and Yours
content:
The BBC has announced it will be cutting a raft of Radio 4 programmes including the long-running consumer and social affairs show You and Yours.
The social sciences show Thinking Allowed will also be cut along with arts and ideas programme Free Thinking, as the corporation seeks £500m savings.
Other shows such The Artificial Human and Open Country will also go, it was announced on Thursday, while Radio 5 Live will also see a reduction in commissioning on its schedule and podcasts.
The BBC has committed to investing in a new consumer programme, though, and two new weekly shows exploring ideas shaping the world, and the impact of technology and AI.
Radio 4's flagship history, science and culture show, In Our Time, will expand in length, as will Start the Week and Farming Today.
Director of BBC Sounds Jonathan Wall said they were "reshaping BBC speech audio" in order to "build a strong future for trusted journalism, distinctive storytelling and programmes that bring people together".
"By commissioning fewer programmes overall, we can focus our investment and make our best shows work across broadcast, on demand and different formats," he said in a statement.
"That means accelerating growth on our own digital platforms and reaching more people beyond the BBC, while maintaining the strength of Radio 4 and 5 Live, the country's two biggest speech radio stations."
He added that the "difficult decisions" about cuts to shows and staff were "not based on cost alone", saying: "We need to make significant savings while investing for the future."
Last month, director general Matt Brittin said the BBC's financial situation and changing audience habits "may well mean" some channels and radio stations have to close so resources can be invested in on-demand services.
Brittin told BBC One's Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg that "we wouldn't guarantee any programme or any channel will exist forever".
In June, the BBC announced 550 job cuts in news, nations and TV and radio content as part of its first stage in its plan to save £500m across the corporation over the next two years.
Staff were told of proposals including ending Radio 4's The World Tonight, and reducing the number of permanent presenters on Today from five to four, with a single anchor on Saturdays.
It was revealed that BBC One's Breakfast would no longer be shown on Sunday mornings, and that the production teams making Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg and Newsnight would merge.
It followed April's announcement that the BBC would cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs - or almost one in 10 - in an attempt to tackle "significant financial pressures".
Last week, an influential group of MPs said the BBC licence fee should be extended to cover services other than TV, and that the corporation's charter review should be scrapped and made permanent.
In its recommendations, the DCMS committee also said that political appointments to the BBC board should end, to improve public trust.

title: How a folk band, football club and Fifa 11 came together for an unlikely terrace anthem
content:
It's a tale as old as time. Take one 16-year-old video game, a rising indie-folk band and a League One football team and what do you get?
A new football anthem for Wycombe Wanderers, courtesy of the unlikely figures of Irish chart-toppers Kingfishr, whose singer was the special guest under the Tuesday night lights of the club's Adams Park stadium this week.
It's a strange musical connection that came about in a way avid fans of sports video games can understand - via Fifa 11, a game the band said they started playing while recording their second album.
The band adopted Wycombe Wanderers as their team in the game and eventually posted a song for the club, which has racked up more than 190,000 views on TikTok .
The club caught wind of the song, written in an Irish folk style and with a lyrical focus on "the Wycombe wanderer, wandering away" and replied to the original post by saying: "You can wander our way anytime."
So it came that lead singer Eddie Keogh took up the offer on Tuesday night, as first reported by Irish sports site Balls.ie , and attended the club's 4-1 EFL Trophy victory over Bristol Rovers.
The song was even playing over the tannoy as he arrived, to the singer's shock as demonstrated by his "what is going on?" post to TikTok .
The club invited him onto the pitch where he was presented with his own club shirt with 'Kingfishr 1' on the back.
In statement to BBC News NI, a Wycombe Wanderers spokesperson said discovering the song was "brilliant".
"As fate would have it, Eddie from the band was able to join us that evening to visit the stadium, watch a game, meet the players and learn a little more about the club he's adopted as his own.
"A lot of our players are massive fans of the band, and the song from the TikTok has gone down extremely well with supporters, so we hope it might become a terrace anthem."
The club spokesperson added that Kingfishr "are welcome back to Adams Park at any time".
It's not the first sporting connection for the band, who first broke big in Ireland due to their viral track Killeagh, a song that has topped the Irish charts on three separate occasions.
The track details a community's attachment to their local Gaelic games club.
The band also played in Londonderry earlier this year where they were presented with shirts belonging to local clubs.
